valveWhenTitle: When should you use a solenoid valve?
valveWhenText: A solenoid valve is a natural choice when you intend to dispense water from a pressurised installation, such as a tap. It allows Autolejek to start and stop the flow without operating a pump.
valveParametersIntro: Before buying, check not only the connection size and allowable pressure, but also the electrical parameters of the coil:
valveSupplyItem: supply and control type: AC or DC,
valveStateItem: the valve's normal state: normally closed (NC) or normally open (NO),
valveDutyItem: permitted duty cycle, including suitability for continuous operation.
valveDutyWarning: Continuous operating time is an often-overlooked parameter. Not every coil may remain energised without interruption—an unsuitable solenoid valve will overheat and may be damaged. Look in the documentation for “100% ED”, “continuous duty”, or an explicit approval for continuous operation.
valvePulseText: Some solenoid valves do not require continuous power to hold their state. A short electrical pulse switches the valve, while a bistable mechanism, permanent magnet, or—in some pilot-operated designs—the fluid pressure differential also helps maintain its position. Closing may require a second pulse, often with reversed polarity.
valvePulseCaveat: Do not assume, however, that an ordinary valve will remain open merely because water is flowing. Pulse or latching operation must be stated explicitly in its documentation, and the control method must be compatible with the Autolejek output.
valveAutolejekTitle: Powering a solenoid valve from Autolejek
valveInputVoltageRange: Autolejek requires a DC supply of at least 6 V and no more than 32 V. Exceeding 32 V DC may damage the controller.
valveAutolejekDc: Relay no. 1 supplies the solenoid valve with the same voltage as the Autolejek input. For a 12 V DC coil, use a 12 V DC supply; for a 24 V DC coil, use a 24 V DC supply. An unusual voltage is also possible if it lies within the 6–32 V DC range and is compatible with every component in the system.
valveAutolejekAc: Relay no. 2 acts as a controlled switch in an independent circuit. A solenoid valve connected to this relay requires a separate, correctly selected power supply. Connecting more than 24 V AC to relay no. 2 is not recommended.
valveCurrentLimitsIntro: The coil current connected to one relay must not exceed 3 A, and its power must not exceed 42 W. The permissible current therefore depends on voltage: it is the lower of 3 A and 42 W divided by the supply voltage.
valveCurrentTableCaption: Maximum coil current resulting from the 3 A and 42 W limits
valveCurrentLimitsCaveat: The table shows output limits, not a recommended normal operating current. Always leave a safety margin, select the fuse for the coil, and account for any inrush current stated by the manufacturer. If a coil exceeds either limit, use a suitably rated external relay or contactor.
valveInductionTitle: The coil, magnetic field, and voltage spike
valveInductionText: A solenoid-valve coil is an inductive component. When current flows through it, a magnetic field forms around the coil, moves the core, and switches the valve. Energy is stored in this field. When the supply is disconnected, the field collapses rapidly and the coil—through self-induction—tries to maintain the existing current.
valveVoltageSpikeIntro: The faster the current is interrupted, the greater the induced voltage can be. Its magnitude is described by
valveVoltageSpikeEffect: The resulting brief spike may be many times higher than the supply voltage and can cause arcing across relay contacts, electromagnetic interference, false pulses in signal cables, or even damage to electronics.
valveFlybackTitle: Flyback diode at a DC coil
valveFlybackText: Autolejek has a built-in diode that protects the circuit against inductive voltage spikes. Even so, for a DC solenoid valve I recommend fitting an additional flyback diode directly across the coil terminals, using the shortest possible leads. When power is switched off, it provides a local path for the decaying current and suppresses the spike at its source.
valveBuiltInDiodeText: Some solenoid valves already contain a flyback diode or another suppression component. Check this in the documentation. A coil with a built-in diode has a defined polarity—reversing its wires may cause a short circuit. If suitable suppression is already installed at the coil, adding a second parallel diode is usually unnecessary.
valveAcSuppressionText: Never connect an ordinary flyback diode in parallel with an AC coil: it would conduct during one half-cycle and cause a short circuit. AC valves require suppression intended for alternating voltage, such as an RC snubber or a correctly rated varistor. Always select the suppressor for the coil type and follow the manufacturer's recommendations.
valveSafetyText: Mains voltage is dangerous. The AC circuit should have a suitable enclosure, protection, and earthing, and it should be installed by a person with the required qualifications.
